paper_title: MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Molecular discovery requires searching vast chemical and biological spaces for candidates that satisfy multiple competing objectives, including potency, binding speciﬁcity, toxicity, structural novelty, and stability [1, 2, 3, 4]. These demands have been traditionally addressed by experimental workﬂows comprised of library preparation, screening, counter-screening, and hit validation [1, 2]. Recently, computational workﬂows have shown great success in molecular design [5, 2, 3]. They often involve diﬀerent molecular representations, model architectures, training objectives, and optimization strategies with the available data [6, 7]. They must also be integrated with evaluation and selection procedures that reﬂect the discovery objectives [1, 2]. Virtual screening, for example, requires jointly considering predictions of activity [8] and toxicity alongside structural constraints [1, 9], while protein design requires the coordination of target preparation, backbone generation [5], sequence 1Northeastern University, Boston, MA, USA; 2Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA; 3Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA; 4Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering, Harvard University, Boston, MA, USA; 5Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA; 6University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA; 7University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada; 8The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA; 9University of Washington, Seattle, WA, USA; 10Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Cambridge, MA, USA; 11Yale University, New Haven, CT, USA; 12Microsoft Research New England, Cambridge, MA, USA; 13Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA; 14Brigham and Womens Hospital and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA. These authors contributed equally. Co-corresponding authors: Tianyu Liu, Yuanqi Du, Nir Hacohen, James J. Collins, and Wengong Jin. Contact: Wengong Jin (wjin@broadinstitute.org). 1 design [4], and evaluation of binding and speciﬁcity [2]. Decisions about both the models and their integration determine which candidates advance to experimental testing [1, 3], making task-speciﬁc model and workﬂow optimization central to successful discovery. Finding an eﬀective workﬂow for given task is challenging search problem [10, 11]. The growing diversity of molecular representations, model architectures, training strategies, and optimization strategies creates vast space of possible conﬁgurations whose performance varies across biological targets, available data, and desired properties (Figure 1a) [6, 3, 7]. Navigating this space requires an eﬀective search policy for designing and training models, evaluating candidate workﬂows, and deciding how to customize them [12, 13]. For human scientists, this policy is shaped by experience across projects. Previous successes and failures provide lessons in workﬂow and model engineering: which architectures suit the available data, which training strategies improve generalization, and which practical constraints must be addressed. These lessons help researchers identify strong starting points and prioritize beneﬁcial changes (Figure 1b). As experience accumulates, scientists can adapt models and workﬂows to new problems with fewer rounds of trial and error. This expertise is particularly valuable, as the evaluation of each candidate requires expensive wet lab validation. Each project can contribute not only workﬂow for given task but also experience that improves the strategy used to develop future workﬂows. Recent advances in scientiﬁc agents have begun to automate aspects of model and workﬂow development that traditionally depend on human expertise [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 13, 19, 20]. Biomni retrieves relevant tools, databases and software from uniﬁed biomedical environment, then uses language model reasoning and code execution to compose them into workﬂows [21]. In protein design, Claude Science has produced experimentally validated binders through campaigns guided by expert-written protocols specifying design objectives and evaluation criteria [22, 23]. Developing and executing these workﬂows produces evidence about which approaches succeed and which attempts fail [17]. However, the reported studies do not establish how this experience improves workﬂow development in subsequent problems. When campaigns remain isolated, lessons from one project cannot inform the search policy for the next. Retaining and applying these lessons across tasks would allow agents to build on earlier work [24, 25] and develop new workﬂows with less repeated trial and error. Here we introduce MolRSI, molecular discovery agent that couples model and workﬂow engineering with persistent cross-task memory to improve its search policy (Figure 1c). The agent converts scientiﬁc methods and associated code into validated, executable skills, then uses experience-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) to assemble and reﬁne candidate workﬂows, including their model architectures and training strategies. Inspired by how experienced researchers draw lessons from past projects, MolRSI records these choices and their outcomes in persistent memory together with the context of each task. Past workﬂow performance and modiﬁcation outcomes guide selection and reﬁnement on subsequent tasks, while records of execution failures and veriﬁed repairs help the agent resolve similar problems. Each search adds to this experience and changes how later models and workﬂows are developed, forming cycle of recursive self-improvement (RSI). We evaluate MolRSI in virtual antibiotic screening and de novo peptideMHC (pMHC) binder design, two challenging problems that require balancing competing objectives. These applications test our hypothesis that systematic optimization of models and workﬂows, guided by experience from previous tasks, can improve discovery under these constraints. In antibiotic discovery, MolRSI draws on experience from 25 molecular property prediction tasks to develop customized screening workﬂow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty. Experimental testing against Staphylococcus aureus identiﬁes 17 of 107 compounds with minimum inhibitory concentrations of 32µg/mL or lower. The observed hit rate of 15.9% is substantially higher than the 8.7% achieved by our previous expert-driven workﬂow using the same training data and screening library [1]. In pMHC binder design, MolRSI draws on experience from 14 minibinder design tasks to develop customized workﬂows for pMHCs. Experimental screening identiﬁes 2 eight hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs, each showing preferential enrichment for its intended target over the tested oﬀ-targets, whereas the workﬂow developed by Claude Science yields no hits. These results highlight the value of accumulated experience and task-speciﬁc optimization for molecular discovery under competing objectives.

sections.title: 2.1 Overview of MolRSI
sections.content: MolRSI combines workﬂow search with persistent memory to implement recursive self-improvement (RSI) for molecular discovery (Figure 1c). Each task speciﬁes biological problem, available data, an evaluation criterion and computational budget. An Explore Agent organizes task-relevant scientiﬁc papers and associated code, tools, benchmarks and algorithms into validated, executable skills. These skills form the resource library from which MolRSI constructs candidate workﬂows. MolRSI develops these workﬂows through experience-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), starting from conﬁgurations assembled from the resource library or retrieved from solution memory. Its search policy determines which workﬂows to explore, how to allocate search eﬀort and how to reﬁne and execute candidates.At each iteration, selection rules draw on workﬂows and scores in solution memory, combining performance on the current and related tasks with an exploration bonus [26] for less-visited alternatives. Reﬁnement memory supplies previous modiﬁcations and their outcomes to guide changes to the selected workﬂow. The agent then executes and evaluates the revised candidate, using execution memory to allocate resources and resolve errors. Search returns the workﬂow with the best development score within the tasks computational budget. Persistent memory carries the outcomes of these searches forward to guide later decisions. Each attempt updates the stored workﬂows, performance scores, modiﬁcation outcomes and execution records. These updates change subsequent search decisions within the task and remain available for later tasks. Search experience can also lead to revised or additional skills. Searches on new tasks therefore use policy informed by earlier outcomes and generate further experience that revises the policy applied to subsequent tasks, completing the RSI cycle (Methods and Sections S1.1 to S1.3). We assess the contribution of this cross-task policy adaptation by comparing MolRSI with and without RSI. Both settings use experiences obtained during the current task to guide search, whereas only MolRSI with RSI also draws on experience from previous tasks. Zero-search transfer tests direct reuse of previously developed workﬂow conﬁgurations without new search. Model ﬁtting on target training data and evaluation on target validation data are retained.

sections.title: 2.2 MolRSI for antibiotic discovery
sections.content: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most pressing global public health threats, steadily eroding our ability to treat common bacterial infections and imposing large and growing burden of mortality worldwide[27]. The spread of antibiotic resistance creates an urgent need for compounds that inhibit bacterial growth while limiting toxicity to human cells. In our previous work [1], we built an expert-driven virtual screening workﬂow that combined ensembles of Chemprop graph neural networks predicting activity against Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) with separate ensembles predicting cytotoxicity in human cell lines such as HepG2. We applied these models to more than 12 million compounds and used additional ﬁlters for undesirable substructures and similarity to known active compounds, followed by graph-based 3 Figure 1: MolRSI motivation and architecture. (b) Scientists accumulate lessons from experimental outcomes across projects, learning to avoid unproductive choices and focus exploration on promising regions. (c) MolRSI couples systematic workﬂow search with persistent cross-task memory. The Explore agent retrieves relevant resources from scientiﬁc literature and code repositories, then converts them into reusable, executable skills through implementation and validation. Workﬂow evaluations update solution memory (workﬂows and performance), reﬁnement memory (modiﬁcations and their eﬀects) and execution memory (execution strategies and repairs). Accumulated experience guides subsequent workﬂow selection, reﬁnement and execution, recursively improving the eﬀective search policy from πt to πt+1. In (a,d,e), means and 1 sample SD are shown across ﬁve data splits. Circles in (a) denote individual splits. analyses that identiﬁed chemical substructures associated with predicted antibacterial activity. This workﬂow enabled the discovery of new structural class of antibiotics. Developing such workﬂows requires navigating interdependent choices in molecular representation, model selection and training, screening criteria and candidate prioritization[6, 1]. We therefore use antibiotic discovery to assess whether MolRSI can autonomously ﬁnd better virtual screening workﬂows and learn from its own searches to improve the search policy applied to subsequent tasks. We ﬁrst benchmark its workﬂow search and then experimentally test compounds selected by the resulting virtual screening workﬂow. MolRSI outperforms existing agents in antibacterial activity prediction benchmarks. Accurate prediction of antibacterial activity is central to prioritizing compounds for experimental testing. We therefore benchmarked MolRSI and existing agents on six antibacterial activity prediction tasks, each corresponding to diﬀerent bacterial species (Figure 2a). We compared MolRSI with the scientiﬁc research agents Biomni, Claude Science and STELLA and general-purpose coding agents Codex and Claude Code [28]. For this comparison, we ﬁrst evaluated MolRSI without RSI, starting each task without experience from previous tasks. This establishes baseline for assessing the contribution of RSI. MolRSI develops workﬂows by selecting and reﬁning combinations of models and methods from the full resource library of 110 reusable skills, comprising 55 models, 48 methods and seven tools or resources (Figure 2b). All agents used the same ﬁve similarity-based data splits. Mean validation area under the precisionrecall curve (AUPRC) guides workﬂow selection, and mean held-out test AUPRC measures predictive performance (Methods and Section S3.1 and supplementary information S2). MolRSI achieves the highest mean test AUPRC among the evaluated agents, ranking ﬁrst on four tasks and second on the remaining two. MolRSIs performance and search eﬃciency improves as it accumulates experience from more tasks. We next tested whether experience from other molecular prediction tasks improves the search policy used to develop antibacterial workﬂows. MolRSI ﬁrst searched independently on 25 source tasks, comprising 22 Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) [29] tasks and three cytotoxicity tasks for HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells[1] (Supplementary Table S3). The six antibacterial benchmark tasks were excluded from this experience pool (Figure 2c). MolRSI used workﬂow performance, reﬁnement outcomes and execution feedback from these searches to guide workﬂow selection, reﬁnement and execution on the antibacterial tasks (Methods and Section S3.2). Under the same search budget, MolRSI generally achieves higher mean test AUPRC than the baseline agents across the search trajectories (Figure 2d). On E. coli and N. gonorrhoeae, its ﬁrst evaluated workﬂow already outperforms the ﬁnal workﬂows selected by every baseline agent after 20 search iterations. To assess the contribution of RSI, we compared searches with and without experience from previous tasks using the same initial resource library, backbone model and search budget (Figure 2e). RSI improves mean test AUPRC on all six antibacterial tasks. We also included zero-search transfer to test whether previously developed workﬂows can be applied without further workﬂow optimization. This setting retains model ﬁtting and validation on target data (Section S3.3). Zero-search transfer outperforms search without RSI on S. aureus, A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae, achieving the highest mean test AUPRC among the three conditions on K. pneumoniae. Experience therefore improves subsequent search and, on several targets, provides workﬂows that outperform search from scratch without further optimization. We further examined whether the beneﬁts of accumulated experience increase as more tasks contribute to it (Figure 2f). We increased the number of source tasks contributing experience from 2 to 25 and assessed workﬂow transfer to the six antibacterial targets. We averaged performance across all combinations containing the same number of source tasks to ensure that the observed trend is not driven by particular task order. The mean test AUPRC of the transferred workﬂows increases from approximately 0.32 with two source tasks to approximately 0.37 with all 25. With experience from all 25 tasks, this performance exceeds the mean AUPRC of 0.361 achieved by search without RSI after 20 iterations. These results show that accumulating experience across more tasks makes increasingly eﬀective workﬂows available for subsequent tasks, extending 6 the beneﬁts of RSI from improved search to better performance (Section S3.2). MolRSI identiﬁes compounds with potent in vitro activity against MRSA. We next evaluated whether the screening workﬂow developed by MolRSI can identify antibacterial compounds while balancing activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty. We used the same training datasets and screening library of approximately 12.1 million compounds as in our previous expert-driven study [1]. The workﬂow integrates optimized antibacterial activity and cytotoxicity predictors with structural ﬁltering and diversity-based selection. Structural ﬁlters exclude speciﬁed antibiotic cores and compounds similar to known antibiotics, while cytotoxicity predictions for HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells inform candidate prioritization. Antibacterial activity ranking followed by selection across structural clusters yields 107 compounds for experimental testing (Figure 3a; Methods; Section S3.4). Experimental validation identiﬁes 17 compounds with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 32µg/mL or lower against methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA). The hits occupy multiple regions of the chemical space (Figure 3b). Among these hits, C3 and C32 also exhibit potent activity against methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), with MICs of 1 and 8µg/mL, respectively. C3 and C32 are ranked at 28th and 5th by predicted antibacterial activity among the tested compounds (Figure 3c). Both compounds inhibit MRSA at concentrations that do not cause cytotoxicity in each of the three types of human cells. Their half-maximal cytotoxic concentrations (CC50) range from 6.4 to 17.5µg/mL for C3 and from 24.2 to 54.7µg/mL for C32. These measurements establish separation between antibacterial potency and mammalian cytotoxicity under the tested conditions (Figure 3d,g; Section S3.6). MolRSI improves experimental hit rate and antibacterial activity prediction over the previous expert-driven workﬂow. The 17 hits among 107 tested compounds correspond to an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% (21 of 241 compounds) in the previous expert-driven study at the same MSSA MIC threshold [1]. Thus, using the same training datasets and screening library, the workﬂow developed by MolRSI achieves an approximately 82% relative increase in observed hit rate (Figure 3e; Section S3.6.3). To assess predictive performance independently of diﬀerences in compound selection, we compared the antibacterial activity predictors on shared held-out set of 271 compounds experimentally evaluated in the previous study (Section S3.1). MolRSI achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.828, compared with 0.590 for the previous predictor, and an area under the precisionrecall curve (AUPRC) of 0.300, compared with 0.090 (Figure 3f). The improved predictive discrimination on common test set complements the higher prospective hit rate, demonstrating gains in both activity prediction and the yield of experimentally active compounds.

sections.title: 2.3 MolRSI for de novo peptide–MHC binder design
sections.content: Class major histocompatibility complex (MHC-I) molecules display intracellular peptides on cell surfaces, providing access to disease-associated antigens for engineered cell therapies and protein therapeutics[2, 31]. Designing binders for these pMHC complexes requires recognition of the exposed peptide while avoiding the same MHC presenting peptides from healthy cells. This task is demanding because target and oﬀ-target complexes share the large MHC scaﬀold and may diﬀer only in few exposed peptide residues. In our previous work, an expert-driven workﬂow combined RFdiﬀusion [5], ProteinMPNN [4] and pMHC-specialized AlphaFold2 model [32, 33] to generate small proteins that contact the presented peptide [2]. The workﬂow produced binders that distinguished target pMHCs from closely related peptide-swapped oﬀ-targets and supported antigen-dependent T-cell activation when used in chimeric antigen receptors. Reaching this outcome required experts to choose peptide hotspots, generation strategies and criteria for both target binding and oﬀ-target discrimination. Here, we use this application to test whether MolRSI can automate and improve this process in three stages: benchmarking binder prioritization across protein targets, applying the 7 Figure 3: Virtual screening and experimental validation with MolRSI. (c) Activity-score ranking of tested compounds. (d) MSSA and MRSA MICs and HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 CC50 values for two selected hits, C3 and C32; dots show individual MIC measurements. (e) Hit rates for 107 MolRSI-selected and 241 expert-selected compounds [1], with 95% Wilson conﬁdence intervals. (f) AUROC and AUPRC on the shared 271-compound held-out S. aureus test set. (g) Chemical structures and doseresponse curves of C3 and C32. Symbols show responses; lines indicate descriptive logistic ﬁts. Two response series are shown per curve. Hits are deﬁned by an MSSA MIC of 32µg/mL or lower. 8 Figure 4: Benchmarking and experience-guided optimization of pMHC binder-design workﬂows. (a) Enrichment Factor (EF) at the top-ranked 1% and 2% cutoﬀs (EF@1% and EF@2%) for MolRSI and four agent baselines across 14 miniproteinbinder tasks. Heatmaps show individual tasks; bars show the unweighted macro average across tasks. (b) Protein resource library organized into input preparation, generation, sequence design and assessment, structure prediction, scoring and score combination. (c) EF@1% and EF@2% on the held-out MART-1 pMHC target for MolRSI with and without RSI and four agent baselines. (d) Best-so-far search objective, deﬁned as the mean ranking score among the top 5% of candidates, during MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 design-workﬂow optimization. (e) On-target versus oﬀ-target scores for selected MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 designs from MolRSI and Claude Science, evaluated with the MolRSI ranking score (left) and Claude Science score (right). accumulated experience to pMHC ranking and prospective design, and experimentally screening the resulting candidates. MolRSI improves binder prioritization than existing agents on 14 target benchmark. Accurate candidate prioritization is central to recovering experimental hits from protein-design campaigns [3]. Across 14 miniprotein targets, MolRSI more eﬀectively prioritizes experimentally conﬁrmed binders than the comparison agents. We asked MolRSI and four leading scientiﬁc or general-purpose agents [21, 34, 35, 36] to rank candidates in experimentally annotated tasks assembled from previous studies [37, 38, 3]. Each task represents diﬀerent protein target, and all agents received the same inputs, objective and computational budget (Sections S2.3 and 4.3.2). We ﬁrst evaluated MolRSI without drawing on experience from previous tasks, while retaining access to the full resource library of 65 executable skills spanning candidate generation, structure prediction and scoring (Figure 4b). We assessed how eﬀectively each workﬂow prioritizes experimentally conﬁrmed binders using the Enrichment Factor (EF) at the top-ranked 1% and 2% of candidates (Section 4.3.1). MolRSI achieved the highest macro EF at both cutoﬀs: 8.01 at 1%, compared with 7.62 for the next-best agent, and 7.29 at 2%, compared with 6.71 for the next-best agent (Figure 4a). Thus, even without prior-task memory, MolRSI develops stronger binder-ranking workﬂow than the comparison agents. Additional benchmark results and comparisons with ﬁxed expert-deﬁned objectives are reported in Sections S4.2 and S4.3. Cross-task experience helps MolRSI develop better pMHC binder design workﬂows. Drawing on experience from the miniprotein tasks, MolRSI achieves better candidate ranking on new pMHC task. MolRSI developed and validated the pMHC ranking workﬂow using two gp100 datasets. MART-1 was reserved to test whether the resulting workﬂow generalizes to an unseen pMHC target (Sections S4.1 and 4.3.1). We compared the resulting workﬂow with those developed by the four agent baselines. MolRSI achieves the highest MART-1 test enrichment, with EF@1% and EF@2% of 3.65 and 5.55, respectively (Figure 4c). None of the comparison agents identiﬁes an experimentally conﬁrmed binder among the top-ranked 1% of candidates, and the highest baseline EF@2% is 1.85. To isolate the contribution of RSI, we also compared against an otherwise identical MolRSI workﬂow search without access to accumulated experience from the 14 miniprotein tasks. Without this experience, the same system achieves an EF of 0.00 at both cutoﬀs. Additional AUPRC and EF results are reported in Section S4.3. We next used the ranking workﬂow developed with accumulated experience to guide pMHC design workﬂow optimization for MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1. For each target, peptide-swapped oﬀ-target retains the same MHC molecule, making peptide discrimination part of the design setting (Sections 4.3.3 and S4.4). MolRSI kept the ranking procedure ﬁxed while conducting 30-round search over generation methods and settings, using the mean score of the top-ranked 5% of candidates as the search objective. The best observed objective reaches 6.76 for MART-1 and 7.56 for SARS-CoV-1, improvements of 66% and 28% over the initial conﬁgurations, respectively (Figure 4d). We then compared the resulting pMHC design pipelines with Claude Science under the same target and oﬀ-target speciﬁcations, design constraints and computational budget. We selected Claude Science for this comparison because it achieves the highest average macro EF among the agent baselines on the miniprotein benchmark and previously demonstrated autonomous design of experimentally validated protein binders [22]. Each agent retained its own design workﬂow (Sections 4.3.3 and S4.5). To compare their outputs, we evaluated the top 500 selected candidates using the ﬁxed MolRSI ranking score and the sum of ipSAEmin z-scores [39] from the three prediction models used by Claude Science. Z-scores were calculated separately for each target and prediction model, pooling candidates from both design methods. By both measures, MolRSI designs have higher median on-target scores than Claude Science designs for MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 (Figure 4e). Prospective experimental screening identiﬁes speciﬁc pMHC binders designed by MolRSI. We next ask whether the computational advantages of MolRSI translate into experimental binding. Minibinders, MHC and peptides are blue, orange and pink, respectively; yellow dashed lines indicate candidate polar contacts. vitro selection against MART-1 (ELAGIGILTV) and SARS-CoV-1 (GLMWLSYFV) pMHCs. Sequencing-based enrichment is quantiﬁed for each designpMHC pair, with hits requiring strong on-target enrichment (log2FC > 4) that exceeds the highest measurable oﬀ-target enrichment. MolRSI yielded ﬁve MART-1 hits among 251 evaluable designs and three SARS-CoV-1 hits among 266, whereas Claude Science yielded no hits among 288 and 267 evaluable designs, respectively. Removing the learned ranking procedure likewise yielded no hits among 479 evaluable designs across the two targets, supporting the contribution of candidate prioritization to experimental success (Figure 5a). This diﬀerence emerged within broadly shared structural landscape: designs from all three methods occupied overlapping regions of the structural-similarity map, while the recovered hits spanned multiple structural neighborhoods (Figure 5b). Experimental hits also tended to receive high MolRSI scores. When evaluable designs from all three groups were ranked together, all ﬁve MART-1 hits 11 fell within the highest-scoring 9% of 767 designs, and the three SARS-CoV-1 hits fell within approximately the highest-scoring quarter of 784 designs, linking the computational score to prospective hit recovery (Figure 5c). Predicted complexes of representative hits, mart1_0014 and sars1_0101, positioned the minibinders over the exposed peptide and suggested contacts with multiple peptide residues, including potential polar interactions (Figure 5d). These models are consistent with the peptide-engaging recognition mode sought by the workﬂow, while the screening results establish experimental enrichment and target preference for designs recovered by MolRSI.

sections.title: 3 Discussion
sections.content: MolRSI improves molecular-discovery workﬂows through recursive self-improvement of the search policy used to develop them. Performance on related tasks changes the selection scores that determine where the agent directs further exploration. Current-task evaluations revise these priorities, while earlier modiﬁcations and execution outcomes guide reﬁnement and repair. The policy therefore changes throughout workﬂow development and carries the eﬀects of earlier searches into subsequent tasks. Those searches produce new results that revise later decisions, completing the recursive process. This links two levels of improvement. At the task level, the agent selects and reﬁnes computational methods to produce an eﬀective workﬂow. Across tasks, the results of these attempts change how it approaches the next search. The computational comparisons show that adapting this policy helps the agent make better use of ﬁxed search budget. Under matched conditions, incorporating prior-task results improves the workﬂows selected for antibacterial prediction and pMHC ranking. The antibacterial search trajectories also show that eﬀective workﬂows can be found early, sometimes exceeding the ﬁnal performance of baseline searches at the ﬁrst evaluation. The resulting workﬂows can also remain useful beyond their original tasks. Direct transfer outperforms search from scratch on several antibacterial targets, providing an additional beneﬁt of earlier workﬂow development. The retrospective pool analysis further identiﬁes better available workﬂows as experience covers more source tasks. Together, these ﬁndings show how earlier searches can supply eﬀective conﬁgurations and improve the policy used to develop new ones. The experimental studies demonstrate why improved workﬂow development matters for molecular discovery. In antibiotic discovery, the MolRSI workﬂow achieves higher observed hit rate than the previous expertdriven workﬂow using the same training data and screening library [1]. Evaluation on shared held-out compound set supports the predictive value of the workﬂow alongside its ability to prioritize active compounds for testing. The pMHC application extends the framework to design, where selecting candidates requires considering both target binding and discrimination against related oﬀ-targets. The ranking workﬂow developed with prior experience guides subsequent generation and selection, yielding binders with preferential binding to their intended complexes over tested oﬀ-targets. The workﬂow developed by Claude Science yields no hits under the same screening conditions. These experiments assess complete workﬂows that coordinate several computational methods. Their outcomes show the practical value of improving how such methods are selected, combined and reﬁned before candidates advance to experimental testing. These results also suggest how scientiﬁc agents that improve through use should be assessed. successful ﬁnal workﬂow establishes performance on particular biological problem. Policy improvement concerns how the agent conducts subsequent searches, including which alternatives it explores and how eﬀectively it uses the available budget. Comparisons between search with prior experience, search from scratch and direct transfer help distinguish the value of inherited conﬁgurations from the beneﬁt of further workﬂow development. This makes the decisions involved in developing workﬂows open to systematic evaluation. Which methods are combined, which modiﬁcations are pursued and which attempts fail all provide evidence that can change later 12 search priorities. Such evidence complements the scientiﬁc knowledge embodied in existing models and tools. Future benchmarks could assess how eﬀectively an agent adapts its search policy over successive tasks. Further progress depends on whether policy updates remain useful as biological targets and evaluation criteria change. The variation among experience pools highlights the importance of the contributing tasks, while current-task evaluation provides way to reassess priorities inherited from earlier searches. Biological validation remains necessary to establish whether better computational scores lead to more eﬀective molecular candidates. Future systems could incorporate experimental outcomes into policy updates, allowing laboratory successes and failures to inﬂuence which workﬂows receive further exploration. This would connect the improvement of search strategies more closely to the biological goals of discovery. More broadly, MolRSI shows that scientiﬁc experience can be transferred between related tasks to improve the policy that guides workﬂow development. This provides basis for discovery systems that reﬁne their search strategies through use, with each project contributing to how future problems are approached.

sections.title: 4.1 MolRSI framework
sections.content: 4.1.1 Resource library construction MolRSI uses an Explore Agent to build the resource library. The agent searches for scientiﬁc papers and their associated code repositories, tools, benchmarks and algorithms relevant to the task. It uses the task description and data characteristics to formulate queries about data representations, model architectures, training objectives and domain constraints. For each retrieved resource, the Explore Agent creates reusable skill describing how to use it. Each skill speciﬁes the resources purpose, software dependencies, input and output requirements and execution steps, with references to available code, documentation and usage examples. The agent checks each skills syntax, dependencies and interfaces during library construction. When newly constructed skill is ﬁrst used for task, the agent runs usage example in an isolated environment. If execution fails, it uses the error messages and repository information to revise the code, dependencies or environment settings, then reruns the example. Skills that pass execution validation are tagged as validated and retained for reuse. Skills that still fail after repair are removed, so that only validated skills are available for subsequent tasks. Full implementation details are given in Section S1.1. 4.1.2 Persistent memory MolRSI retains experience from workﬂow development and evaluation in solution, reﬁnement and execution memory. These memories are updated during each task and retained for use in later tasks. MolRSI uses the accumulated experience to guide later iterations of the same search and searches on new tasks. Experience from previous tasks could also be used to select an existing workﬂow without new search, mode referred to as zero-search transfer. Solution memory. Solution memory stores each workﬂows executable code, conﬁguration, execution status and any available development scores. Development scores are calculated using the task-speciﬁc evaluation criterion to compare workﬂows during search. The conﬁguration speciﬁes the component methods, data processing, model architecture, parameter settings and training or generation procedures. Each score is stored with the task, dataset, evaluation metric, and data split and random seed identiﬁers where applicable. MolRSI uses the stored workﬂows and scores to select workﬂows for further reﬁnement on the current task or transfer to new task. 13 Reﬁnement memory. Reﬁnement memory stores the original and revised workﬂows, the changes made and the reasons for proposing them. For revisions that complete evaluation, it also stores the development scores before and after the change, measured under the same task-speciﬁc evaluation protocol, and their diﬀerence. Modiﬁcations are retained whether performance improves, declines or remains unchanged. Revisions that fail during execution are stored with their failure status. MolRSI uses these previous modiﬁcations and their outcomes when proposing further changes on the current task or related tasks. Execution memory. Execution memory stores the computational requirements of workﬂows and the skills available in the resource library. Runtime, GPU time, processing speed and GPU memory use are stored together with the dataset, dataset size, hardware conﬁguration and software environment. MolRSI uses these measurements and their associated execution conditions to plan computing resources for later runs. When execution fails, execution memory stores the stage at which the failure occurs, the error messages and logs, and the cause when identiﬁed. It also stores each attempted repair, including changes to code, dependencies, environment settings or resource allocation, and whether the repair succeeds. When similar errors occur in the same or later tasks, MolRSI retrieves the previous repairs and their outcomes to guide further debugging. Details of memory storage and updates are given in Section S1.2. 4.1.3 Recursive self-improvement of the search policy MolRSI uses experience from its own workﬂow searches to improve its search policy. Evaluation results from the current task and experience retained in persistent memory guide which workﬂows to explore, which modiﬁcations to pursue and how to resolve execution failures. Each attempt provides further evidence about workﬂow performance, the eﬀects of modiﬁcations and execution requirements. This experience informs subsequent search decisions within and across tasks, completing the feedback loop through which recursive self-improvement occurs. Workﬂow search uses experience-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) [26]. Initial workﬂows form the roots of separate trees, with each node representing workﬂow. workﬂow selected for modiﬁcation is the parent, and revised version is its child. Workﬂows based on common model or computational approach are grouped into families. Each search iteration comprises the following ﬁve steps: Step 1: Selecting workﬂow families. MolRSI selects workﬂow family using current task performance, an exploration bonus and historical transfer score. For families already evaluated on the current task, the performance term uses the best development score obtained in earlier iterations. The exploration bonus [26] is larger for less visited families. The historical transfer score summarizes the familys performance on related tasks using solution memory. Historical experience guides initial exploration, and current task scores are incorporated as evaluations become available. The family with the highest combined score is selected. The selection rule and historical transfer score calculations are given in Section S1.3. Step 2: Selecting parent workﬂows. MolRSI samples parent workﬂow from those already evaluated on the current task. Sampling favours better development performance, penalizes workﬂows that have already produced more candidates, and incorporates historical transfer scores from solution memory. The sampling rule and eligibility criteria are given in Section S1.3. Step 3: Proposing workﬂow modiﬁcations. MolRSI retrieves previous modiﬁcations and their outcomes on related tasks from reﬁnement memory. It uses these modiﬁcations and outcomes to propose changes to the selected parent workﬂow, such as replacing method, changing how components are combined or adjusting parameter settings. Each proposal speciﬁes the changes and their rationale. Before execution, MolRSI checks that the proposed workﬂow follows the required format, does not duplicate an existing candidate and is feasible to run. 14 Step 4: Executing and evaluating workﬂows. Using the resource requirements stored in execution memory, MolRSI conﬁgures the runtime environment and allocates computing resources. It then runs the revised workﬂow and assesses its performance using the task-speciﬁc evaluation procedure. If execution fails, MolRSI ﬁrst searches execution memory for similar errors and the repairs that have resolved them. When relevant experience is available, it uses the previous repair to guide changes to the code, dependencies or environment settings. Otherwise, it diagnoses the problem from the current error messages and makes the necessary changes. The workﬂow is rerun after each repair. If execution still fails, MolRSI uses the new error messages to guide further changes, up to predeﬁned limit on repair attempts and within the tasks computational limits. Successful evaluations provide development scores for subsequent search iterations. Step 5: Updating search policy to guide subsequent searches. After each execution attempt, MolRSI stores the workﬂow, its execution status and any available development score in solution memory. It adds the modiﬁcation and its outcome to reﬁnement memory and stores runtime, resource use, errors and repair outcomes in execution memory. MolRSI then uses the updated memories to select families and parents, propose modiﬁcations, allocate resources and repair execution failures in later iterations (Steps 14). We denote the eﬀective policy governing the decisions in Steps 14 by πt(a s), the distribution over search actions for the current task and search state s. Let Mt denote persistent memory after updates and Et the new execution and evaluation experience. The policy before and after memory update is expressed as πt(a s) = π(a s; Mt), Mt+1 = Update(Mt, Et), πt+1(a s) = π(a s; Mt+1). (1) The updated policy guides further searches, whose results supply experience for the next memory update (Figure 1). This feedback loop implements recursive self-improvement of the eﬀective search policy. MolRSI uses the outcomes of its own searches to focus exploration on promising workﬂows, reduce repeated unsuccessful modiﬁcations and reuse eﬀective repairs. The same process operates within task and across tasks as experience accumulates. Search stops when the task-speciﬁc limit on evaluation attempts or computation time is reached. MolRSI returns the successfully evaluated workﬂow with the best development score on the current task. MolRSI uses experience from previous tasks to select workﬂow for direct transfer or as the starting point for new search. It ﬁrst identiﬁes the best matching previously completed task, referred to as the source task, using task type, evaluation metric, dataset size and task description similarity. It then retrieves the workﬂow with the best development score on that source task from solution memory. In zero-search mode, the retrieved conﬁguration is applied to the new task without searching over alternative workﬂows. Model parameters are ﬁtted using the new tasks training data where required. Alternatively, the retrieved workﬂow serves as the starting point for further search using Steps 15, within the task-speciﬁc limits on evaluation attempts or computation time.

sections.title: 4.2 MolRSI for antibiotic discovery
sections.content: 4.2.1 Datasets and benchmark evaluation Source tasks for experience accumulation. We used 25 source tasks to accumulate experience for antibiotic workﬂow development: 22 absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity tasks from the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) [29], together with three cytotoxicity tasks for HepG2, HSkMC and 15 IMR-90 cells from our previous study[1]. The TDC tasks used the oﬃcial benchmark partitions and taskspeciﬁc evaluation metrics. The cytotoxicity datasets were obtained from our previous study, with the same compound structures and experimental measurements. Each cytotoxicity dataset was divided into training, validation and test sets at proportions of 8:1:1 using molecular similarity, with Tanimoto threshold of 0.40. Five splits were generated using diﬀerent random seeds. Antibacterial target tasks. We evaluated MolRSI on six antibacterial activity prediction tasks for Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. These tasks were excluded from the source experience pool. The datasets were obtained from our previous study, with the same compound structures and experimental measurements. Each dataset used ﬁve similarity-based training, validation and test splits with Tanimoto threshold of 0.40, proportions of 8:1:1 and the same ﬁve random seeds used for the cytotoxicity tasks. All methods used identical splits. Each task involved single workﬂow search, during which every candidate was ﬁtted and evaluated across all ﬁve splits. Mean validation AUPRC guided the search, and the workﬂow with the highest value was selected. Test AUPRC is reported as the mean and sample standard deviation across the ﬁve splits. Test outcomes were not used to guide workﬂow search. Activity S. aureus held-out test set. For the predictive comparison in Figure 3f, we used held-out set of 271 compounds from our previous study [1]. This set comprised 241 candidate compounds and 30 low predicted activity controls; the 12 known antibiotic class positive controls were excluded. MolRSI and the published antibacterial activity model were evaluated on the same compounds using the same experimental activity labels. AUROC and AUPRC are reported for both models. Dataset sizes and evaluation metrics for all datasets are provided in Section S3.1, together with the split sizes and random seeds used for workﬂow development. We benchmarked MolRSI with RSI and MolRSI without RSI against Biomni, Claude Science, STELLA, Codex and Claude Code on the six antibacterial target tasks (Figure 2). All agents received the same task prompt, datasets and development objective, with up to 20 attempted workﬂow evaluations per task. Each agent retained its native tools and workﬂow development procedures. MolRSI and all agent baselines except Codex used Claude Sonnet 5; Codex used GPT-5.5. MolRSI accessed its backbone model through the Anthropic API, whereas Biomni ran on its own platform. Complete task prompts, model identiﬁers, API settings and baseline conﬁgurations are provided in Section S2.2. 4.2.2 Evaluation of recursive self-improvement MolRSI searched for workﬂows independently on the 25 source tasks described in Section 4.2.1. Experience from these searches was pooled in persistent memory before evaluation on the antibacterial target tasks. We compared MolRSI with and without RSI. MolRSI with RSI began with the accumulated source memory, whereas MolRSI without RSI began without experience from previous tasks. Both conditions used the same resource library and backbone model, together with the data partitions, evaluation procedure and workﬂow evaluation budget speciﬁed in Section 4.2.1. Memory was updated during each search to guide subsequent iterations. Experience generated on one antibacterial task was not passed to the other antibacterial tasks. For the search trajectories in Figure 2d, we identiﬁed the workﬂow with the highest mean validation AUPRC obtained so far at each iteration. Its test performance was calculated after the search to construct the plotted trajectory. For zero-search transfer (Figure 2e), MolRSI ﬁrst identiﬁed the best matching source task using task type, evaluation metric, dataset size and task description similarity. It then selected the workﬂow with the best validation performance on that source task. Both selections were made before evaluating the workﬂow on the antibacterial task. Model parameters were ﬁtted using the target tasks training data where required, and the transferred workﬂow was evaluated without further workﬂow search. We compared the transfer performance available from diﬀerent numbers of source tasks with the performance of MolRSI without RSI after workﬂow search (Figure 2f). One workﬂow from each of the 25 source tasks was transferred to each antibacterial task, yielding 150 source target evaluations. Experience pools contained 225 source tasks. For each pool, the transfer test AUPRC on each antibacterial task was identiﬁed retrospectively, and these values were averaged across the six tasks. The mean was calculated over all source task combinations of each size, with variation among combinations estimated from 2,000 random orderings of the source tasks. The transfer evaluations and calculation of means and percentile ranges are described in Section S3.2. 4.2.3 Virtual screening and compound selection MolRSI uses the experience accumulated across source tasks to guide the development of virtual screening workﬂow for identifying candidate antibiotics against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The workﬂow combines antibacterial activity prediction with cytotoxicity prediction for HepG2, HSkMC and IMR-90 cells. The activity models were trained on methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA; strain RN4220). All activity and cytotoxicity models used the same training datasets as our previous study [1] and both studies used the same screening library. Screening began with structural ﬁltering. Compounds with maximum Tanimoto similarity of 0.40 or greater to the antibacterial reference set were excluded. Structural ﬁltering also removed compounds matching PAINS [42] or Brenk alerts [43] and speciﬁed antibiotic cores. Cytotoxicity was then predicted separately for the three cell types. The HepG2 and IMR-90 predictors combined MiniMol embeddings [44] with Morgan ﬁngerprints [45] and RDKit descriptors [46], whereas the HSkMC predictor used MiniMol embeddings. Cytotoxicity ﬁltering used score threshold of 0.40 for each cell type. Model architectures, reference compounds and ﬁlter settings are described in Section S3.4. The remaining compounds were ranked by weighted combination of predictions from two MiniMolbased variants and LANTERNRADR ensemble, with weights of 0.55, 0.30 and 0.15, respectively. Each component prediction was averaged across ﬁve ﬁtted models. Butina clustering [47] grouped structurally similar compounds, and candidates were selected across clusters to retain chemical diversity. We selected and experimentally tested 107 compounds. Activity against MRSA was assessed during experimental validation. Compound identities, prediction scores and sourcing details, including supplier substitutions and exceptions to the cytotoxicity criterion, are provided in Section S3.4. 4.2.4 Experimental validation Antibacterial activity assays. Antibacterial activity was measured against methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus RN4220 (MSSA; DSM 26309) and methicillin-resistant S. aureus USA300 FPR3757 (MRSA; ATCC BAA-1556). Compounds were ﬁrst screened at single dose of 128 µg mL1, and those that inhibited growth were advanced to two-fold doseresponse testing from 128 µg mL1 (89 concentrations, to 1 or 0.5 µg mL1). Overnight LB cultures grown from single colonies were diluted to approximately 105 CFU mL1 in fresh LB and added to plates containing compound in DMSO (ﬁnal DMSO 1%). Plates were covered with lid and incubated for 1824 at 37 with 5% CO2. Growth was measured as OD600. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was deﬁned as the lowest concentration giving 90% growth inhibition relative to untreated growth controls, and compounds with an MSSA MIC 32 µg mL1 were deﬁned as hits. DMSO vehicle, untreated growth and Triton X-100 kill controls were included. MICs were determined in technical replicate (n = 2-3) in single experiment, and the higher replicate value was reported. 17 Cytotoxicity assays. Cytotoxicity was measured in human hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2; ATCC HB8065), primary human skeletal muscle (HSkMC; ATCC PCS-950-010) and human fetal lung ﬁbroblast (IMR-90; ATCC CCL-186) cells. Cells were seeded at 510 103 cells per well in 96-well clear ﬂat-bottom black tissue-culture-treated plates (100 µL per well) and incubated for 24 at 37 and 5% CO2 before dosing. Compounds were added as two-fold dilution series from 128 to 0.5 µg mL1, with 1% DMSO at the highest concentration diluted in step with compound, and cells were incubated for 4872 h. Viability was quantiﬁed with PrestoBlue HS (10 µL per well, 4 at 37 C) by ﬂuorescence (excitation/emission, 550/590 nm). Untreated cells deﬁned 100% viability, with matched DMSO series and Triton X-100 (0.1%) lysis wells as vehicle and ﬂoor controls and media-only wells as background. The half-maximal cytotoxic concentration (CC50) was calculated by log-linear interpolation between the two concentrations bracketing 50% viability. Each compound and concentration was tested in two technical wells in single experiment.

sections.title: 4.3 MolRSI for peptide–MHC binder design
sections.content: 4.3.1 Datasets and benchmark evaluation The protein study instantiated the cross-task update framework in three stages. First, ranking workﬂow development on 14 miniprotein-binder tasks supplied protein-domain source experience. Second, MolRSI used the resulting experience memory to develop workﬂows for one pMHC binder design task. Third, the selected pMHC workﬂow guided prospective binder design workﬂow optimization for MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHC complexes. Miniprotein-binder tasks. We assembled experimentally annotated de novo miniprotein-binder datasets for 14 protein targets from three published studies [37, 38, 3]. Each target deﬁned task using leave-one-target-out partition: workﬂow search used the other 13 targets, and the selected workﬂow was then evaluated on the held-out target. We retained all 1,565 positive designs and sampled up to ten negatives per positive within each target, yielding 17,215 designs. Target identities, sample counts and label deﬁnitions are reported in Section S4.1. pMHC task. The pMHC benchmark comprised three target datasets: two for gp100 and one for MART-1. Both gp100 datasets were used directly for workﬂow search, while MART-1 was reserved for testing. Each candidate was represented as four-chain complex comprising the HLA heavy chain, β2-microglobulin, the presented peptide and the designed binder. The datasets were generated using the experimental screening procedure described by Liu et al. [2]. Peptide identities, dataset sizes and label deﬁnitions are reported in Section S4.1. Ranking metrics. We evaluated candidate rankings using the area under the precisionrecall curve (AUPRC), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the Enrichment Factor (EF). EF measures the positive fraction among top-ranked candidates relative to the positive fraction in the full target dataset. For target with candidates and N+ experimentally positive binders, let nf be the number retained at the top-ranked fraction and n+,f the number of positives among them. We calculated EFf = n+,f /nf N+/N , {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1}. (2) We denote these metrics as EF@1%, EF@2%, EF@5% and EF@10%, respectively. Random ranking has an expected EF of 1. At each cutoﬀ, macro EF is the unweighted average across the 14 miniprotein tasks (Figure 4a). For the pMHC benchmark, EF is reported separately for the held-out MART-1 target (Figure 4c). Full EF results at all four cutoﬀs and AUPRC results are reported in Section S4.3. Comparisons with ﬁxed expert-deﬁned scoring criteria are provided in Section S4.2. 18 Design targets. We designed binders for HLA-A*02:01 complexes presenting MART-1 (ELAGIGILTV) and SARS-CoV1 (GLMWLSYFV). Each intended pMHC was paired with an oﬀ-target complex presenting diﬀerent peptide while retaining the same HLA heavy chain and β2-microglobulin. Target sequences and exposed peptide hotspots were derived from source structures. The source coordinates were not supplied as design inputs. Oﬀ-target peptide sequences, source structures and hotspot deﬁnitions are given in Supplementary Table S14. 4.3.2 Evaluation of recursive self-improvement Resource library and workﬂow search. MolRSI selected and conﬁgured components from the protein resource library, which contained 65 executable skills comprising 28 models and 37 registered scoring terms (Figure 4b). For ranking workﬂow development, these components covered input and feature preparation, complex-structure prediction, sequence and interface scoring, and score aggregation. Each candidate workﬂow mapped targetbinder pair to scalar ranking score. AUPRC on development data from the 13 non-held-out targets guided workﬂow search and selection within each miniprotein-binder task, whereas AUROC guided search and selection for the single pMHC task. Benchmark baselines and budget. We compared MolRSI with Biomni [21], Claude Science [34], STELLA [35] and Codex [36]. For each benchmark task, all agents received the same task inputs, data partitions, and evaluation objective, with budget of 300 A100 GPU-hours and 20 attempted workﬂow evaluations. Each agent retained its native tools and workﬂow-development procedures. Folded structures and the scores produced by each model were cached and reused across workﬂow evaluations to avoid repeated computation. Task instructions and baseline conﬁgurations are provided in Supplementary Information S2 and section S2.3. Memory ablation. We compared pMHC workﬂow search initialized with pooled experience from the 14 miniprotein-binder tasks against search without this prior experience. The initial memory contained no pMHC or prospective design outcomes. Both conditions used identical resource libraries, candidate data, search controllers, evaluation objectives and procedures, and the per-task budget speciﬁed above. Memory was updated during search in both conditions, so the comparison isolated the contribution of prior cross-task experience. 4.3.3 Binder generation and candidate selection Generation-workﬂow optimization. The prospective pipeline combined candidate generation, hotspotcontact ﬁltering, inverse folding and ranking. MolRSI optimized generation methods and conﬁgurations separately for each target, using RFDiﬀusion3 [48], Proteina-Complexa [49], PXDesign [50], BoltzGen [51] and the MOSAIC [52] simplex accelerated proximal gradient method (APGM). Each target-speciﬁc search received up to 30 attempted rounds and 1,000 A100 GPU-hours. The searches ran in parallel without sharing evaluations or search records. For each evaluated conﬁguration, we generated 20 backbones with binder lengths of 80120 residues. SolubleMPNN [53] generated eight sequences per retained backbone, with cysteine excluded from the sequence alphabet. The ranking procedure selected in the memory-guided pMHC search remained ﬁxed throughout prospective search and candidate selection. The mean score among the top-ranked 5% of generated candidates served as the conﬁguration-selection objective. Final candidate generation and selection. After each target-speciﬁc search, the three highest-scoring workﬂows each generated 8,000 additional designs. Candidates from the search and expansion stages were pooled and deduplicated. Final MolRSI candidates were required to satisfy on_target_ipsae_min 0.50, monomer_plddt 0.80, at least 15 HLA contacts (hla_res_contact 15), and son soff > 0. Passing 19 designs were ranked by the on-target frozen-veriﬁer score son. Experimental outcomes are reported separately over evaluable designs, as deﬁned below. Detailed generation and selection settings are provided in Section S4.4. The Claude Science protocol is described in Sections S2.3 and S4.5. 4.3.4 Experimental validation Biotinylated pMHC monomers were purchased from KACTUS Bio and comprised HLA-A*02:01 (Gly25 Thr305), β2-microglobulin (Ile21Met119) and the MART-1 (ELAGIGILTV) and SARS-CoV-1 (GLMWLSYFV) peptide. Binder designs were synthesized by Twist Biosciences and cloned into engineered M13 bacteriophage lacking gIII as previously described [54]. Phage libraries were then selected for speciﬁc binding activity using host E. coli cells encoding positive selection circuits for on-target pMHC binding activity and negative selection circuits for oﬀ-target pMHC binding using an adaptation of previously described methods [55, 56]. Next generation sequencing of phage-encoded designs was used to assess enrichment of functional designs throughout selection.

sections.title: Data Availability
sections.content: The molecular property prediction, antibacterial activity, human-cell cytotoxicity and miniprotein-binder datasets used for computational workﬂow development and benchmarking are publicly available. Molecularproperty prediction datasets were obtained from the Therapeutics Data Commons [29]. Antibacterial activity and human-cell cytotoxicity datasets, including the 271-compound held-out S. aureus test set, were obtained from our previous study [1]. Miniprotein-binder datasets were obtained from the studies by Cao et al. [37, 38] and Bennett et al. [3]. The pMHC binder datasets from Liu et al. [2] are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request. Dataset sources, composition and partitions are described in Sections S3.1 and S4.1.
