Supplementary Table S12 and Supplementary Table S13 report EF at four cutoﬀs and AUPRC. 33 S1 MolRSI framework S1.1 Resource library construction Resource retrieval and synthesis. The Explore Agent generates task-speciﬁc queries about scientiﬁc methods, software and benchmark evaluation using the task description and available dataset information. It searches literature and web sources, removes duplicate results and ranks the remaining resources by relevance to the task. The retrieved material is summarized to identify models, methods, tools, benchmarks and associated implementations for skill construction. Resource analysis and skill construction. The Explore Agent examines the retrieved resources and their available code, documentation and usage examples. It prioritizes resources for skill construction according to task relevance and the requested skill categories. When repository code is available, static analysis of Python abstract syntax trees recovers public interfaces and their arguments. These interfaces, together with model deﬁnitions and training or inference examples, inform the skill instructions. Additional searches supply supporting repositories or documentation when the initial material is incomplete. Library organization and skill contents. shared index lists each skills name, category and purpose. Each skill describes how to use the resource and links these instructions to available implementations, dependencies, usage examples and source references. Where relevant, it also speciﬁes feature representations and whether computed features could be reused. The contents are summarized in Supplementary Table S1. Checks during construction. The Explore Agent checks package identity and examines Python usage examples for syntax and import-name inconsistencies. When an execution environment is available, it also checks dependency availability and selected interfaces. Detected problems prompt revisions to installation instructions, dependencies or usage examples. These checks precede execution validation when skill is ﬁrst used. Execution validation and reuse. When newly constructed skill is ﬁrst used, MolRSI runs usage example in an isolated environment. Execution errors guide repairs to the code, dependencies or environment settings. The example is rerun until it completes successfully or reaches the repair-attempt limit. Skills that pass are tagged as validated and retained in the resource library for reuse. Skills that remain unsuccessful are removed. Incremental expansion. The Explore Agent could expand an existing resource library by retrieving additional resources and identifying skills not already present. Existing skills are retained. New skills undergo the same construction checks and ﬁrst-use execution validation, and the shared index is updated to include them. S1.2 Persistent memory Workﬂow development generates experience about candidate performance, proposed modiﬁcations and execution. MolRSI retains this experience in solution, reﬁnement and execution memory, together with the tasks and conditions under which it was obtained. These memories guide later search decisions within and across tasks (Supplementary Figure S1). Solution memory. For each evaluated workﬂow, solution memory stores the task description, task type, dataset and dataset size, together with the workﬂows executable code, conﬁguration and execution status. The conﬁguration speciﬁes the workﬂow family, component models and methods, architecture, hyperparameters, data processing, training objective and training or generation procedure. Development scores are retained with their evaluation metric and, where applicable, data split and random seed. workﬂow that failed before evaluation retains its failure status without receiving development score. Scores from completed workﬂows provide evidence about which families performed well on related tasks and which individual workﬂows are 34 Table S1: Contents of the resource library. The shared index identiﬁes available skills. Each skill combines instructions with the implementation, source information and validation results available for that resource. The supporting material depends on the resource. Component Shared index Skill instructions Implementation Source information Interfaces and examples Validation information Information provided Skill names, categories, purposes and links to the corresponding instructions. Resource description, intended use, installation, supported operations and usage examples. Available source code, model deﬁnitions, dependencies and supporting scripts. Scientiﬁc references, repository location, revision and package information. Available operations and examples of feature extraction, model ﬁtting or inference, as appropriate to the resource. Validation status, checks performed and their outcomes. suitable for further reﬁnement or transfer. The historical score normalization, family selection and parent selection procedures are speciﬁed in Section S1.3. Reﬁnement memory. Reﬁnement memory stores the original workﬂow, the revised workﬂow, the task and the proposed changes. Changes are described by the aﬀected component and its settings, such as an architecture change, the use of parameter-eﬃcient ﬁne-tuning, diﬀerent loss function, altered data processing or change in learning rate. The agents reason for proposing change is retained alongside the result of testing it. When the original and revised workﬂows are evaluated under the same protocol, both development scores and their diﬀerence are stored. Improvements, declines, unchanged scores and execution failures are all retained. If proposal changes several components, its outcome is associated with the combined modiﬁcation. For subsequent proposal, the agent retrieves relevant earlier changes and their outcomes, including previous attempts derived from the selected parent workﬂow. Execution memory. Execution memory stores the execution history of workﬂows and the usable skills in the resource library. For each attempt, it retains the dataset and its size, hardware and software environment, execution status and available runtime measurements. Resource measurements include elapsed time, GPU time, processing speed and GPU memory use. Where measured, training time per sample per epoch relates runtime to dataset size and training duration. These measurements inform later resource allocation and timeout settings. For each failure, the memory retains the failed stage, error messages, execution logs and the cause when identiﬁed. It also stores each attempted repair, including changes to code, dependencies or environment settings, and whether re-execution succeeded. This experience guides repairs when similar errors recur. Updates within and across tasks. Memory is updated after each execution attempt and used to guide subsequent iterations. Experience retained from completed tasks could also guide later searches or direct workﬂow transfer. When an evaluation used ﬁxed source-task experience, each target began with the same experience, and updates from one target were not shared with other targets. Application-speciﬁc experience pools are described in Sections S3.2 and S4.1. Held-out test scores are excluded from memory updates and search decisions. Section S1.3 describes how the updated memory guides the search policy. 35 S1.3 Recursive self-improvement of the search policy Search representation. MolRSI uses experience-guided Monte Carlo tree search over forest of executable workﬂows. Initial workﬂows form the roots of separate trees, and each node represents concrete workﬂow with its speciﬁcation, execution status, development scores, resource use, logs and generated artifacts. workﬂow selected for modiﬁcation is the parent, and the revised workﬂow is its child. An edge represents the proposed changes, such as diﬀerent representation, architecture, objective, data-processing procedure or composition of methods. Workﬂows based on common model or computational approach are grouped into families. The ﬁve steps below specify how current-task observations and historical experience guide search decisions. Step 1: Selecting workﬂow families. Family selection combines the best available current-task development performance, an exploration bonus and historical transfer score. Historical workﬂow scores are ﬁrst standardized within each source task and then aggregated using task-similarity weights. The family-level score enters selection as an additive term. corresponding workﬂow-level historical score enters parent sampling in Step 2 as multiplicative factor. The normalization and aggregation used by both steps are deﬁned together below. Historical score normalization. Let xτ (v) denote the development score of workﬂow on source task τ , and let Vτ contain completed workﬂows with ﬁnite development scores on that task. Scores are ﬁrst oriented so that larger values indicate better performance: sτ (v) = xτ (v), xτ (v), for higher-is-better metric, for lower-is-better metric. Each score is then normalized relative to the other completed workﬂows on the same source task: esτ (v) = sτ (v) medianu Vτ sτ (u) max{MADu Vτ (sτ (u)), ϵ} . (3) (4) Here, MAD(s) = median median(s) is the median absolute deviation from the median, and ϵ > 0 prevents division by zero. The normalized score is mapped to bounded utility: sτ (v) = 2σ(esτ (v)) 1, σ(x) = 1 1 + ex . (5) The resulting utility lies in [1, 1], allowing historical outcomes measured on diﬀerent scales to be aggregated without an unbounded contribution from single task. All scores used in this calculation were available during development of the source workﬂow; held-out test scores are excluded. Task-similarity weights. For target task τ0, the contribution of source task τ is weighted according to evaluation-metric compatibility, task type, dataset size and task-description similarity: w(τ, τ0) = wmetric(τ, τ0) wtype(τ, τ0) wsize(τ, τ0) wemb(τ, τ0). (6) The non-negative factors wmetric and wtype encode compatibility of evaluation metrics and task types. Datasetsize similarity is calculated as wsize(τ, τ0) = exp[γ log Dτ log Dτ0] , where Dτ denotes the dataset size associated with task τ , and γ > 0 controls the penalty for size diﬀerences. Description similarity is calculated from task-description embeddings eτ and eτ0 : (7) wemb(τ, τ0) = max{cos(eτ , eτ0), 0} . (8) 36 Family and workﬂow transfer scores. Let Tf denote the eligible source tasks containing an evaluated workﬂow from family , and let Vτ,f denote the evaluated workﬂows from that family on source task τ . The family-level transfer score is transfer(f ) = τ Tf w(τ, τ0) meanv Vτ,f sτ (v) τ Tf w(τ, τ0) . (9) This calculation ﬁrst averages performance within each source task and then combines those task-level averages. For target-task workﬂow vi, let Ti denote source tasks containing an eligible historical match. The matching rule uses workﬂow family and modiﬁcation type, and matched(vi, τ ) denotes the historical workﬂow identiﬁed on source task τ . The workﬂow-level transfer score is τ Ti transfer(vi) = w(τ, τ0) sτ (matched(vi, τ )) w(τ, τ0) τ Ti . (10) Tasks without an eligible record are excluded from the corresponding numerator and denominator. These weighted averages are deﬁned when the total task weight is positive. With non-negative task weights and utilities in [1, 1], each deﬁned transfer score also lies in [1, 1]. Family-selection rule. Let index family-selection decisions, Feligible denote the eligible workﬂow families and nb(f ) 1 denote the visit count for family . The next family is selected according to fb = arg max Feligible exploitb(f ) } {z current-task performance + α t ln(b + 1) nb(f ) {z exploration bonus } + transfer(f ) . } {z historical transfer (11) The exploitation term summarizes the best current-task development performance within family , including stability and overﬁtting adjustments, on scale from zero to one. The coeﬃcient α controls exploration, with larger bonuses for less-visited families [2]. Historical evidence enters through the family-level transfer score deﬁned above. Historical experience guides initial exploration, and current-task scores are incorporated as evaluations become available. Step 2: Selecting parent workﬂows. Let contain completed, non-ensemble workﬂows with ﬁnite development scores on the current task. For workﬂow vi V, let qi denote the current-task score supplied to the sampler and ci the number of existing children. Sampling weights and probabilities are β wi = σ qi medianvj qj MADvj V(qj), ϵ max 1 1 + ci [1 + λ transfer(vi)] , p(vi) = wi wj . vj (12) The coeﬃcient β controls sensitivity to standardized current-task scores. The factor 1/(1 + ci) reduces repeated expansion of the same parent, and λ controls the contribution of historical transfer. The normalized sampler requires non-negative weights and positive total weight. 37 Step 3: Proposing workﬂow modiﬁcations. The agent retrieves previous modiﬁcations, their rationales and their outcomes from reﬁnement memory to guide changes to the selected parent workﬂow. Each proposal speciﬁes the changes and their rationale. The proposed workﬂow is checked for the required format, duplication of an existing candidate and feasibility of execution. Malformed, duplicate or infeasible proposals do not become completed workﬂow nodes. The proposed modiﬁcation and its observed outcome are added to reﬁnement memory after execution, including changes that reduced performance or failed to execute. Step 4: Executing and evaluating workﬂows. The proposed child workﬂow is implemented and run in an isolated environment using the task-speciﬁc evaluation procedure. Execution memory informs environment settings and resource allocation. If setup or execution fails, the agent ﬁrst searches execution memory for similar errors and successful repairs. Relevant experience guides changes to the code, dependencies or environment settings. If no suitable repair is available or the problem persists, the agent diagnoses the current failure and proposes further changes. The workﬂow is rerun after each repair, within the repair-attempt limit and computational budget. Successful evaluations supply development scores; all attempts retain their execution status, logs, resource measurements and repair outcomes. Failed evaluations count toward the workﬂow-evaluation allowance, but repairs of the same candidate do not consume additional evaluations. Step 5: Updating search policy to guide subsequent searches. After each attempt, MolRSI adds the workﬂow and its development score or failure status to solution memory. It stores the proposed modiﬁcation and its outcome in reﬁnement memory, and runtime, resource use, errors and repair outcomes in execution memory. The corresponding node and edge in the search forest are also updated. The updated memories guide subsequent family selection, parent sampling, modiﬁcation proposals and execution. These updates change the eﬀective search policy πt, whose subsequent evaluations generate experience for the next memory update. This feedback implements the RSI loop expressed by Mt, Et and πt in Equation (1). Historical and current task updates. Current task executions update development scores, visit counts and the experience used for subsequent reﬁnement and execution. When the source memory was ﬁxed for an evaluation, its historical transfer scores remained unchanged during that target-task search. Under continued use across tasks, experience from newly completed tasks could contribute to transfer estimates for later searches. The bounded transfer scores serve as empirical selection priors; their boundedness alone does not establish standard target-task or node-level regret guarantee. Search termination and returned workﬂow. Search stops when the task-speciﬁc limit on evaluation attempts or computation time is reached. MolRSI returns the successfully evaluated workﬂow with the best current-task development score. This is the best evaluated workﬂow under the stated criterion and budget, rather than global optimum. The evaluation unit and accounting for failed attempts and repairs are speciﬁed in Supplementary Information S2. Workﬂow transfer with and without further search. MolRSI could use experience from previous tasks to retrieve workﬂow for direct transfer or initialize new search. It ﬁrst identiﬁes the best matching previously completed task using task type, evaluation metric, dataset size and task description similarity. It then retrieves that source tasks workﬂow with the best development score from solution memory. This source task routing is distinct from the familyand workﬂow-level transfer scores used in Steps 1 and 2. In zero-search mode, the retrieved conﬁguration is applied to the new task without proposing or comparing alternative workﬂows. Model parameters are ﬁtted using the new tasks training data where required, and ﬁtting and execution still incur computational cost. Alternatively, the retrieved workﬂow becomes starting point for Steps 15 under the new tasks limits on evaluation attempts and computation time. 38 S2 Comparison with baseline agents S2.1 Shared evaluation protocol Agents and comparison settings. We compared MolRSI with Biomni [3], Claude Science [4], STELLA [5] and Codex [6] on antibacterial prediction and protein binder ranking workﬂow development. The antibacterial benchmark additionally included Claude Code [7]. Within each benchmark, agents received the same task inputs, permitted development data, evaluation objective and workﬂow-evaluation allowance. Each agent used its native tools and workﬂow development procedures without common predeﬁned workﬂow search space. The task-speciﬁc instructions and permitted tools are described below. Task instructions and permitted tools. For baseline searches in antibacterial prediction and protein ranking, prompts speciﬁed the task inputs, ﬁxed data partitions, development objective and metric, evaluation allowance, required outputs and permitted tools. No starting prediction model or ranking workﬂow was prescribed. The instructions prohibited changes to the ﬁxed data, partitions, and data-loading or evaluation code, hidden candidate evaluations, and the use of held-out labels or performance for workﬂow development or selection. Independent baseline runs also prohibited reuse of results, code or model choices from another baseline run. Search permissions and execution records. These baseline agents could search using their native capabilities, and local agents could install software packages. Search, installation, environment inspection and deterministic feature caching independent of the labels did not consume candidate evaluations. Candidates were evaluated sequentially, with subsequent choices based on the preceding development results. Each candidates code, outputs, execution status, logs, runtime, development scores and held-out test predictions were retained. Evaluation allowance and repair. candidate counted as one workﬂow evaluation once its evaluation began, including evaluations that failed or timed out. Repair attempts for the same candidate did not count as additional workﬂow evaluations. The authors supplied the task inputs and evaluation interfaces without selecting workﬂow components, repairing candidates or granting additional retries during the runs. LLM backbones. MolRSI used Claude Sonnet 5 throughout the antibacterial and protein studies. In the antibacterial prediction and protein ranking benchmarks, the baseline agents also used Claude Sonnet 5, except Codex, which used GPT-5.5. Claude Science used Claude Opus 5 for prospective binder design. API access and agent interfaces. MolRSI accessed its model through the Anthropic API. Biomni ran on its own platform and used its platform-provided environment for workﬂow planning and execution. Its outputs were not independently reproduced outside that platform. Claude Science used its scientiﬁc workﬂow-development interface. STELLA ran in self-evolve mode using the implementation available at https://github.com/asfarasimconcerned/STELLA. Codex and Claude Code [7] used their native codingagent interfaces, with writable workﬂow directories and ﬁxed data and evaluation helpers. Computational resources. Across antibacterial prediction, protein ranking and prospective binder design, the authors provided GPUs to agent baselines, and each agent controlled job scheduling and GPU use within its task-speciﬁc budget. Their prompts imposed no hard wall-clock limit. These hardware assignments describe the four local baselines and do not specify the resources provided by the Biomni platform. Systems received the same molecular inputs, ﬁxed partitions, development 39 objective and allowance of 20 attempted workﬂow evaluations per task. completed candidate evaluation covered all ﬁve ﬁxed splits in Section S3.1, rather than counting each split as separate attempt. Mean validation AUPRC guided search and ﬁnal workﬂow selection; test predictions were scored after search. Search permissions and execution records. S3.2 Evaluation of recursive self-improvement Source experience. MolRSI developed workﬂows independently on each of the 25 source tasks and pooled the resulting experience in solution, reﬁnement and execution memory. Each antibacterial target began with the same pooled source experience. Experience generated during target search guided later iterations of that search and was not shared with the other targets. Resource library and RSI conditions. The small-molecule resource library contained 110 reusable skills: 55 models, 48 methods and seven tools or resources. These covered molecular standardization, feature construction, predictive models, class-imbalance handling, calibration, stacking and ensembling. MolRSI with RSI and MolRSI without RSI used the same resource library, backbone model, data partitions, evaluation procedure and 20-attempt search allowance. MolRSI with RSI began with the pooled source experience; MolRSI without RSI began without experience from previous tasks. In both conditions, memory was updated during the current task to guide later iterations. Search trajectories. At each iteration, we identiﬁed the completed workﬂow with the highest mean validation AUPRC obtained so far. Its test performance was calculated after workﬂow search to construct the trajectory in Figure 2d. Test scores were not returned to the agent as feedback and were excluded from memory updates. For Figure 2e, MolRSI identiﬁed the best-matching source task using task type, evaluation metric, dataset size and task-description similarity, and then selected the workﬂow with the validation performance on that source task. Screening proceeded through structural novelty ﬁltering, cytotoxicity ﬁltering, activity ranking, Butina clustering and diverse picking (Supplementary Figure S2). Butina clustering [21] grouped structurally similar candidates, and diverse picking selected compounds across clusters to retain chemical diversity. BoltzGen [28], BindCraft [29], and PXDesign [30] are complete binder design pipelines. For the retrospective ranking benchmarks, we isolated ﬁxed loss or ranking criterion used internally by each pipeline and evaluated it retrospectively on the same targetbinder sequence pairs. Thus, these references compare the criteria used to prioritize designs. BoltzGen used its worst-rank quality criterion on Boltz-2 [31] predictions. If rij is the within-target percentile rank of candidate under metric j, with smaller ranks better, the reported higher-is-better score was qi = maxj rij. The primary three-metric reference used equal rank weights for design_iiptm (which restricts the design side of the pTM calculation to residues within 8 Å of the target), design_ptm, and the negative minimum design-to-target PAE. This is the conﬁdence-only form of the BoltzGen criterion. The complete pipeline additionally ranks PLIP [32] hydrogen bonds, PLIP salt bridges, and SASA. We evaluated both the three-conﬁdence-score and six-score forms and report the former as the stronger, and therefore more conservative, ﬁxed comparator. For BindCraft, we reproduced the default eight-term default_4stage_multimer design loss, LBindCraft = 0.1 ℓpLDDT + 0.4 ℓPAE + 0.1 ℓiPAE + 1.0 ℓcontact + 1.0 ℓinterface contact + 0.3 ℓRg + 0.05 ℓipTM 0.3 ℓhelix, with the termini-distance loss disabled as in the default conﬁguration. Terms were evaluated from AlphaFold2Multimer-v3 [33] predictions with target-chain MSAs. The benchmark score was LBindCraft, so that larger values were better. For PXDesign, we reproduced the seven-term PXDesign-h hallucination loss on Protenix-Mini [34] predictions, LPXDesign = 0.15 ℓpLDDT + 0.4 ℓPAE + 0.1 ℓiPAE + 1.0 ℓcontact + 1.0 ℓinterface contact 0.3 ℓhelix + 0.3 ℓRg, and again used its negative as the higher-is-better benchmark score. It should therefore be interpreted as comparison of ﬁxed internal objectives from the three design pipelines rather than an end-to-end comparison of the pipelines themselves. Each prospective design task was speciﬁed by an HLA allele, an on-target and oﬀ-target peptide pair, source structures for sequence and hotspot provenance, chain assignments, binder-length range, and exposed peptide hotspots (Supplementary Table S14). Within each target pair, the HLA heavy-chain and β2-microglobulin sequences were held ﬁxed and only the peptide sequence was changed. The source PDB coordinates were not supplied as design inputs. They were used only to establish the target-chain sequences and select peptide hotspots. Following previous work [27], hotspots were selected from solvent-exposed, upward-facing peptide residues with relative solvent-accessible surface area (relSASA) of at least 20% in the binder-free pMHC complex. Individual binder lengths were sampled within the target-speciﬁc allowed range. Generation workﬂow search conﬁguration. The available generation methods were RFDiﬀusion3 [36], Proteina-Complexa [37], PXDesign [30], BoltzGen [28], and the MOSAIC [38] simplex accelerated proximal gradient method (APGM). The methods diﬀered at the generation stage and entered the same inverse-folding and ranking procedure. The target-speciﬁc searches ran in parallel without exchanging evaluations or search records. Each search was allocated 30 attempted rounds and 1,000 A100 GPU-hours. At each node, MolRSI evaluated generator conﬁguration by generating 20 backbones and applying SolubleMPNN [39] to generate eight sequences for each retained backbone, followed by the remaining scoring steps. Cysteine was excluded from the inversefolding sequence alphabet in all workﬂows. The ranking score among the top-ranked 5% of designs deﬁned the conﬁgurations development reward. After the 30-round search for each target, the three highest-scoring workﬂows were each used to generate 8,000 additional designs. The ﬁnal candidate pool comprised all designs from the search and expansion stages and was then subjected to deduplication, ﬁltering, and ranking. We denote the exported ﬁelds on_target_ranking_score and off_target_ranking_score by son and soff, respectively. For ﬁnal MolRSI selection, designs were retained when on_ipsae_min 0.50, monomer_plddt 0.80, at least 15 HLA contacts (hla_res 15), and s8_on s8_off > 0. Passing designs were ranked by s8_on. 63 S4.5 Comparison with reference design workﬂows Prospective agent comparison. We selected Claude Science as the prospective baseline because it achieved the highest performance on the miniprotein-binder benchmark and had previously demonstrated autonomous design of experimentally validated protein binders [8]. The completed comparison comprised independent target-speciﬁc campaigns for MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1. The target and peptide-swapped oﬀ-target speciﬁcations, binder-length range, design objectives and total computational budget were held ﬁxed, while each system retained its native generation, reﬁnement and ranking procedure. Both systems received 1,000 A100 GPU-hours per target. The 30-round allowance applied to MolRSIs workﬂow search; Claude Science instead controlled job scheduling within the shared GPU-hour budget. Claude Science run conﬁguration for prospective binder design. We initialized one independent Claude Science session per target, using Claude Opus 5 and an adaptation of Anthropics multi-target binder-design protocol [8]. The prompt source is provided in Section S2.3; this section summarizes the study-speciﬁc adaptations and run conﬁguration. We adapted the instructions to peptide-speciﬁc pMHC design and the available computing platform. Inputs comprised HLA heavy-chain and β2-microglobulin sequences and MSAs, onand oﬀ-target peptide sequences, an 80120-residue binder range, epitope hints and novelty references. Every scoring prediction was required to include the HLA heavy chain, β2-microglobulin, peptide and binder. Epitope positions were hints, not mandatory hotspot-contact ﬁlter. The campaign was given computational budget of 1,000 A100 GPU-hours per target, with job state recorded in ﬁles on shared volume. SolubleMPNN [39] and SolubleCaliby [40] were named for designs selected for the ﬁnal computational output, with their base variants permitted during backbone search. The speciﬁed pipeline placed checks for sequence and structural novelty, liabilities, monomer foldability, structural plausibility and redundancy before any complex prediction. The instructions required retained candidates to be scored against the onand oﬀ-target complexes using ESMFold2-Fast, ESMFold2-Full [35] and Protenix v2 [41]. For each scoring model, the ﬁxed criterion combined minimum ipSAE [42], design-to-prediction scDockQ [43] and the on-target-minus-oﬀ-target minimum-ipSAE diﬀerence. Scores were standardized within the candidate cohort and combined with relative weights of 4:1:4. The minimum scDockQ across the scoring models used also entered the ranking key at prespeciﬁed pose threshold of 0.23, ordering designs that met it above those that did not. At least two rounds of partial diﬀusion, prediction followed by redesign, or sequence resampling were required. The requested output was ranked set of 500 designs per target, excluding exact and near duplicates and limiting representation from individual design lineages and structural clusters. At least three structure generators had to be represented, with no more than 50% of designs from one generator or two-thirds from one sequence-design method. The authors speciﬁed the target inputs, scoring criterion, output format, diversity limits and computational budget. Claude Science chose the generation strategy and parameters, sampling allocation, use of epitope hints, monomer and structural-plausibility thresholds, parent selection and reﬁnement operations. The monomer and structural-plausibility thresholds were ﬁxed after selection. The comparison therefore used its native binder-design protocol with pMHCand platform-speciﬁc adaptations.
